text: Hashing, digital signatures, and PKI are three pieces of the same puzzle: proving data is genuine and hasn't been tampered with, without ever needing to share a secret in the clear. Together they're exactly what makes the padlock icon in your browser mean something real, rather than just a decoration.

A hash function takes any input — a password, a file, an entire disk image — and produces a fixed-length output, like SHA-256's 256 bits. The same input always produces the same hash, but even one changed character produces a completely different one, and there is no mathematical way to reverse a hash back into the original input — that's by design, not a limitation. That's why a system should store only the hash of your password, never the password itself, and why publishing a file's hash lets anyone confirm their download wasn't corrupted or tampered with in transit.

A digital signature combines hashing with asymmetric encryption. The sender hashes their message, then encrypts that hash with their own private key — that's the signature. Anyone holding the sender's public key can decrypt it back to the hash, hash the message themselves, and compare. A match proves two things at once: the message really came from that sender, and nothing in it has changed since.

A public key alone doesn't prove whose it is, which is the problem PKI solves. A certificate authority signs a digital certificate that binds a site's public key to a verified identity. Your browser already trusts a built-in list of root authorities, so when a site presents a certificate signed back to one of those roots, your browser can verify the whole chain of trust without ever having met that site before.
That closes out authentication, authorization, and cryptography basics. Next up, Chapter 6 turns to the attacks themselves, starting with malware: viruses, worms, trojans, and ransomware.
